notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Deuteronomy 8, drawn from the sources I was able to access and read in full.

---

## Deuteronomy 8 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter divides naturally into three movements: (1) the lesson of the wilderness — humility and dependence (vv. 1–5); (2) the goodness of the promised land and the call to grateful remembrance (vv. 6–10); (3) the danger of prosperity — pride, forgetfulness, and self-congratulation (vv. 11–20). Meredith Kline calls v. 17 the “focal point” of the chapter — the proud claim “My power and the might of my hand have gained me this wealth.” Moses insists that the memory of God’s wilderness provision is the corrective. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-8-commentary)

Warren Wiersbe notes the three essentials for Israel’s success: listening to God’s Word, remembering it, and obeying it. Four times Moses says “remember” (8:2, 18; 9:7, 27) and four times he says “forget not” (8:11, 14, 19; 9:7). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-8-commentary)

---

### v. 1 — Obedience, Life, and Possession

**Traditional reading:** “Every commandment” (singular in Hebrew, *mitsvah*) refers to the whole body of covenant stipulations, not merely isolated rules. Obedience is the pathway to life, multiplication, and possession — not automatic, but a “golden chain” where commands lead to careful obedience, which leads to life and inheritance. The same pattern appears in Deuteronomy 4:1; 5:1; and 6:1.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** God’s dealings with Israel in the wilderness were disciplinary. By afflictions *and* by benefits, God sought to bring them into humble dependence, submissive obedience, and hopeful trust. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Ellicott:** “Go in and possess” refers not merely to crossing the Jordan under Joshua but to the detailed, ongoing work of possession that Joshua left for Israel after initial establishment (Joshua 13:1, 7). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Precept Austin (NET Note):** The singular *mitsvah* includes the whole corpus of stipulations; the plural form in v. 2 refers to individual stipulations. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-8-commentary)

---

### v. 2 — Remembering the Wilderness as Humble Testing

**Traditional reading:** The 40 years were not wasted time. God led Israel *in order to* humble and test them. The goal of testing was “to know what was in your heart” — not because God lacked knowledge, but so that Israel would come to know themselves.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik), citing G. Campbell Morgan:** “It is important that we recognize that the meaning of this passage is not that God might know them, but that they might come to know themselves. God knows man perfectly. The important thing is that man should come to know himself.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-8/)
- **Ellicott:** “‘To know’ is not simply that He might know… but that the knowledge may arise — to determine, disclose, discover.” He compares 2 Chronicles 32:31 (God testing Hezekiah). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Precept Austin (Jack Deere):** God’s “knowing” is an anthropomorphism; the point is that obedience or disobedience had to be *proven in history*. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-8-commentary)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** God proves people not only by hard commands and mighty works but also by afflictions and calamities (Judges 2:22; Psalm 17:3; 81:7) and by benefits (Exodus 16:4). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)

---

### v. 3 — Manna, Hunger, and the Word

**Traditional reading:** God humbled Israel by letting them hunger, then fed them with something utterly unknown — manna. The lesson: physical bread sustains physical life, but true life — spiritual life — comes from everything that proceeds from God’s mouth. This is the verse Jesus quoted against Satan in the wilderness (Matthew 4:4).

- **John Piper (Desiring God, Reformed Baptist):** Jesus’ quotation of this verse in Matthew 4 shows He is the new Israel, led by the Spirit into the wilderness for 40 days (corresponding to 40 years), tested and hungry. Where Israel failed, Jesus succeeded by trusting God’s word rather than seizing bread by His own power. “The aim of fasting is that we come to rely less on food and more on God himself.” Piper emphasizes that God gave manna *after* letting them hunger — an utterly unheard-of food — precisely so they would learn that bread is not ultimate. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/man-shall-not-live-on-bread-alone)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik, citing Spurgeon):** Spurgeon stresses we must *live on* the word, not fight with it. “The worst implement with which you can knock a man down is the Bible; it is intended for us to live upon — not to be the weapon of our controversies, but our daily food.” Also: believers need the word like bread — for life, growth, and strength; we must feed on it constantly. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-8/)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** “Every word” literally means “all, everything whatever — that proceedeth out of the mouth of the Lord,” i.e., all means God has by His word provided or can provide. The manna is not to be identified with any natural product; it was truly bread from heaven. The name “manna” comes from *man hoo* (“What is it?”). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Precept Austin (John MacArthur note):** “Israel’s food in the wilderness was decreed by the Word of God. They had manna because it came by God’s command; therefore, ultimately it was not bread that kept them alive, but God’s Word.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-8-commentary)
- **Precept Austin (Wiersbe):** Manna was also a type of Christ, the true bread from heaven (John 6:35). The daily gathering taught daily dependence. “Our relationship to the Word of God (manna) indicates our relationship to the God of the Word.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-8-commentary)

---

### v. 4 — Miraculous Preservation of Clothing and Feet

**Traditional reading:** God not only fed Israel supernaturally but preserved their clothing from wearing out and their feet from injury during 40 years of desert travel.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Rejects the naturalistic explanation (that Israel had sufficient flocks and skilled artisans to make new clothes) as “too insignificant beside the miraculous manna.” The Hebrew literally says the clothing “did not fall away, waste away from upon thee.” The verb for the foot does not mean “swell” but suggests softening or being bruised; the meaning is “thy foot did not get into a bruised and wounded state” — because God preserved their sandals from wearing out (cf. Deuteronomy 29:5). Also dismisses as fanciful the rabbinic legend that children’s garments grew with them like snail shells. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Notes that Ginzberg records strange rabbinic legends about these garments — that angels clothed each Israelite in a robe of purple at the exodus that remained ever new, grew with them, could not be harmed by fire, and never bred vermin. Guzik presents this as legend, not as reliable interpretation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-8/)
- **Ellicott:** Offers a spiritual reading: God provides “raiment that waxes not old” in the everlasting righteousness of Christ and good works prepared for us, and those who wait on the Lord “shall walk, and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/8.htm)

---

### v. 5 — Fatherly Discipline

**Traditional reading:** The wilderness hardships were fatherly discipline, not divine hostility. The Hebrew verb (*yasar*) refers to training, education and correction — more like severe discipline than mere punishment. This verse undergirds the New Testament teaching in Hebrews 12:5–11.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** “The idea is not so much that of punishment or chastisement, properly so called, as that of severe discipline and training. God made them feel his hand upon them, but ever for their good.” The end was that they would keep His commandments and walk in His ways (cf. Hebrews 12:5ff). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Ellicott:** “All our ideas of training necessarily imply time; it cannot be done in a moment. But the main point of the illustration is to prove God’s love. ‘Whom the Lord loveth, He chasteneth;’ else, why should He be at the pains to chasten at all?” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/8.htm)

---

### v. 6 — Therefore Keep the Commandments

**Traditional reading:** Because God has disciplined them as a father, the fitting response is obedience, walking in God’s ways, and fearing Him. This is the conclusion drawn from vv. 1–5. Obedience flows from the recognition of God’s fatherly care.

- The Pulpit Commentary connects this to v. 5: the end of the fatherly discipline is keeping commandments, walking in His ways, and fearing Him — so as to enjoy His favour. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)

---

### vv. 7–9 — The Good Land Described

**Traditional reading:** The land is painted in vivid contrast to the wilderness: well-watered (“brooks, fountains and springs”), fertile (wheat, barley, vines, figs, pomegranates, olive oil, honey), mineral-rich (iron in the stones, copper in the hills), and lacking nothing. This description would have been breathtaking to a people who had known only desert.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Brooks are running streams and mountain torrents; fountains are perennial springs; “depths” refers to deep pools or inland lakes (Sea of Galilee, Lake Huleh). Palestine has been celebrated in all ages for corn, wine, and oil. “Honey” (*d’bash*) can refer to bee honey or to grape syrup (*dibs*), still made by Arabs by boiling down grape juice. The contrast with Numbers 20:5 (where the people complained of “no place of figs, or of vines, or of pomegranates”) is deliberate. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik, citing Thompson):** “The reference to iron and copper in the hills is remarkably exact. Ancient copper mines and smelters have been discovered in recent years in the Arabah below the Dead Sea.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-8/)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik, citing Merrill):** “No more graphically beautiful landscape of Canaan exists than in the word picture Moses painted here.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-8/)
- **Ellicott:** Notes the sad irony: “it is a long time since any one has seen Palestine in that condition. Its desolation, no less than its beauty, is a proof of the truth of the Divine word.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/8.htm)

---

### v. 10 — Bless the LORD When Satisfied

**Traditional reading:** Eating and being satisfied is not the danger — forgetting the Giver is. The divine reflex should be to bless (thank) the LORD. This verse is the basis for the Jewish practice of saying grace after meals (*Birkat HaMazon*).

- **Pulpit Commentary:** “From this place the Jews have made it a general rule, or, as they call it, an affirmative precept, that every one bless God at their meals.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Ellicott:** Quotes the Talmud (*Berachoth* 35a): “It is forbidden to any man to take any enjoyment from this present world without thanksgiving; and every one who does so is a transgressor.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Precept Austin:** Notes the text says “WHEN” not “if” — Israel will certainly eat and be satisfied. Their “divine reflex (not ritual) from their heart was to be to bless the LORD for everything they had.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-8-commentary)

---

### vv. 11–14 — The Danger of Forgetting in Prosperity

**Traditional reading:** Moses warns that prosperity creates the conditions for amnesia about God. The chain is: eat and be full → build fine houses → herds, flocks, silver, gold multiply → heart becomes proud → forget the LORD who delivered from Egypt. Verses 11–18 in Hebrew are one long, breathless sentence (Ellicott). The caution is prophetic: Rehoboam, Uzziah, and Hezekiah all fell into exactly this pattern (2 Chronicles 12:1; 26:16; 32:25).

- **John Piper (Desiring God, Reformed Baptist):** “The prosperity of the promised land is so dangerous to our souls that only the recollection of some sobering wilderness weaknesses and wonders will pert the river of our self-sufficiency and pride from flooding our lives and drowning our faith.” God’s purpose in the wilderness was “to make the people intensely, deeply, and lastingly conscious of their total dependence on God for everything.” (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/can-god-spread-a-table-in-the-wilderness)
- **John MacArthur (GTY, Conservative Evangelical):** “Prosperity is its own curse, you know. It makes it so easy for us to forget.” (https://www.gty.org/sermons/1395/the-reality-of-our-salvation)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik, citing Trapp):** “Solomon’s wealth did him more hurt than ever his wisdom did him good.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-8/)
- **Ellicott:** Lists historical fulfillments: Rehoboam forsook the law after strengthening himself; Uzziah’s heart was lifted up to his destruction when strong; Hezekiah “rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** “Wealth is apt to engender in the possessor of it a spirit of self-gratulation and pride… and to be forgetful of the bounteous hand from which all that they enjoy has come.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)

---

### vv. 15–16 — Recalling the Wilderness Dangers and Provision

**Traditional reading:** Moses reminds them of the terror of the wilderness — fiery serpents (named for the burning pain of their bite, probably the cerastes or a naja species), scorpions, drought, no water — and God’s miraculous provision: water from flinty rock, manna. All of this was designed “to humble you and test you, so that in the end He might cause you to prosper” (v. 16).

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The “fiery serpent” and “scorpion” (singular in Hebrew) stand in apposition to “the wilderness” and illustrate its terribleness. The grand end was “to do thee good at thy latter end” — not the end of life (as Numbers 23:10) but the state after the period of discipline. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Ellicott:** Distinguishes the two rocks: the rock at Horeb is called *tsûr* (suggesting hardness); the rock at Kadesh is *selagh* (a cliff or height, suggesting inaccessibility). “Flint” (*challâmîsh*) appears also in Deuteronomy 32:13, Job 28:9, and Psalm 114:8. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Precept Austin:** Emphasizes the full-circle summary: God’s humbling and testing was “to do good for you in the end.” It was training for when they would be “weaned” from manna upon entering the land. “Note that God did not humble them and test them to humiliate them or ruin them but to do good for them.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-8-commentary)

---

### vv. 17–18 — “My Power” vs. God’s Gift

**Traditional reading:** The heart’s proud whisper — “My power and the might of my hand have gained me this wealth” — is the core danger (Meredith Kline identifies v. 17 as the focal point of the chapter). The antidote is to “remember the LORD your God, for it is He who gives you power to get wealth.” God gives the body, brain, talent, and opportunity. The wealth is given “that He may confirm His covenant” — wealth is not an end in itself but serves God’s covenant purposes.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** “The proud claim that one’s own power and might is the true source of one’s wealth is more commonly believed in the heart than said with the lips.” Citing Thompson: “Such a claim is an arrogant elevation of self to the status of God.” Also: “the people of God have no fundamental right to use their material blessing to further selfish purposes.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-8/)
- **John MacArthur (GTY):** On v. 18 — “All money is God’s. Secondly, God grants to men the power to get that which is His.” (https://www.gty.org/sermons/1223/the-christian-and-his-finances)
- **John Piper (Desiring God):** God gave them wilderness experiences “which would make it impossible for a reasonable person to say, ‘My power, my might, or my hand has gotten me this wealth.’” The good God aimed at was not the wealth itself but making them “intensely, deeply, and lastingly conscious of their total dependence on God for everything.” (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/can-god-spread-a-table-in-the-wilderness)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** “They were to ascribe all to God’s gracious bounty, for from him had come the power by which prosperity had been gained, and this he had given, not on account of any merit in them, but that he might fulfill his covenant engagements to their fathers.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)

---

### vv. 19–20 — The Penalty of Forgetting: Perish Like the Nations

**Traditional reading:** Moses stands as a loving but uncompromising witness: if Israel forgets God and follows other gods, they will perish just like the nations God is destroying before them. There is no special immunity. God would eventually use other nations to drive Israel out of the land (the exile), until He restored them.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** “Israel would be tempted to look at the nations being judged in front of them, and to think, ‘We’re better than them, so we are safe. God would never deal with us that way.’ But God would deal with them that way if they rose up in pride against Him.” Pride is “the most Satanic of sins because it was by pride that Satan himself fell.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-8/)
- **Ellicott:** Notes that the word for disobedience in v. 20 (“because ye would not be obedient”) is the same word used positively in Deuteronomy 7:12 — marking off Deuteronomy 7:12–8:20 as a complete section of the discourse. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Moses “enforces his counsel by reminding them again that only destruction awaited them should they forget the Lord their God and apostatize from him (cf. Deuteronomy 4:25ff; 6:14).” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed / Reformed Baptist (Piper, Desiring God)

John Piper’s treatment of Deuteronomy 8 emphasizes God’s absolute sovereignty in the wilderness testing. He reads Israel’s 40 years and Jesus’ 40 days in parallel: God deliberately leads His people into places of hunger and dependence to strip away self-reliance. For Piper, the “good” God aimed at was not material prosperity but deep, lasting consciousness of dependence on God. Wealth is a dangerous test, not a guaranteed covenant blessing for the faithful. “The explicit purpose that God had in leading his people into the wilderness… is given in Deuteronomy 8:16: ‘to humble you, and to test you, and to do you good in the end.’” (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/can-god-spread-a-table-in-the-wilderness)

### Conservative Evangelical / Baptist (MacArthur, GTY)

John MacArthur draws from Deuteronomy 8 to emphasize the danger of forgetting, the sufficiency of Scripture as “bread,” and that all wealth belongs to God. He cites Deuteronomy 8:3 to teach that “every word out of God’s mouth is bread — it feeds somebody.” On v. 18 he stresses two points: all money is God’s, and God grants the power to acquire it. He warns that “prosperity is its own curse” because it makes forgetfulness easy. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/1223/the-christian-and-his-finances) and (https://www.gty.org/sermons/55-18/the-work-of-the-word-part-1)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (David Guzik, Enduring Word)

Guzik’s commentary (widely used in charismatic and Pentecostal circles) treats the chapter as a practical warning against pride. He emphasizes that God’s humbling is for our self-knowledge, that believers need Scripture the way they need bread, and that pride is “the most Satanic of sins.” On v. 18, he teaches that God gives power to gain wealth *for covenant purposes*, and that wealth is not for selfish ends. Guzik does not spiritualise away the material blessings of vv. 7–9; he sees God genuinely wanting to “materially bless a spiritually obedient Israel,” yet he insists the principle is “seek first the kingdom” (Matthew 6:33). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-8/)

**Key difference on v. 18 between traditions:** Reformed teachers (Piper) tend to see the “good” God aimed at as spiritual maturity and dependence, not the wealth itself. Pentecostal/charismatic teachers (Guzik) affirm God genuinely wants to bless materially but insist the blessing must not become an idol. MacArthur stands closer to the Reformed view on the danger of wealth but affirms God as the giver of the power to earn it. None of the sources I read endorse a “prosperity gospel” reading that treats wealth as an automatic sign of covenant faithfulness.

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible Notes, cited via Precept Austin)

The NET Bible notes (cited in Precept Austin) observe that the singular “commandment” (*mitsvah*) in v. 1 refers to the whole covenant corpus, while the plural in vv. 2 and 6 designates individual stipulations. The ESV Study Bible observes that “this chapter makes clear that the wilderness period was not only a punishment but also a test” and that “the land itself is also a test” — the wilderness lesson must be applied in the land. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-8-commentary)

### Jewish Tradition (cited in Pulpit and Ellicott)

- The rabbinic idea that children’s garments grew with them like snail shells is noted and dismissed as fanciful by the Pulpit Commentary. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- The Talmud (*Berachoth* 35a) derives the duty of saying grace after meals from v. 10: “It is forbidden to any man to take any enjoyment from this present world without thanksgiving.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/8.htm)
- The name “manna” derives from the Hebrew *man hoo* (“What is it?”), the Israelites’ bewildered question upon first seeing it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/8.htm)
